name: Baikeno, as one of 'all known Uab Meto varieties'
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Edwards, Owen. 2016. Parallel sound correspondences in Uab Meto. Oceanic Linguistics 55(1): 52-86. DOI 10.1353/ol.2016.0008. Open copy: ANU Open Research, hdl 1885/108661. Corroborated (cluster-level) by Culhane, Kirsten & Owen Edwards. 2025. Consonant epenthesis in Meto. In Rarities in phonetics and phonology, 165-217. Language Science Press, pp. 169, 173; and Edwards, Owen. 2021. Rote-Meto comparative dictionary. ANU Press, ch. 2 p. 36.
catalog_locator: Edwards 2016 p. 55 (journal pagination), section 2 'Uab Meto language background';of 36. Corroboration: Culhane & Edwards 2025 (pp. 169 with fn. 3, 173); Edwards 2021 (p. 36).
catalog_quote: Baikeno data were mainly collected by Charles Grimes (between 2005 and 2015) and are supplemented by data collected during the 2012 Kupang workshop. ... All known Uab Meto varieties have the ten consonants /p t k ʔ b f s h m n/ and either of the liquids /r/ or /l/. ... Known varieties of Uab Meto have the five vowels /i e a o u/. Word stress falls on the penultimate vowel. Vowel-initial words begin with a predictable glottal stop; /asu/ ‘dog’ → [ˈʔasʊ]. While all Uab Meto varieties appear to share the same phoneme inventory, the segments in each variety have different distributions and behaviors. [Edwards 2016: 55; footnote superscripts 4-7 dropped, line-break hyphenation joined] || Meto demonstrates acoustic evidence for stress – specifically from vowel quality, spectral tilt and pitch rise/fall ratios – on the penultimate syllable of the word (Culhane 2024). Syllable weight is not relevant for any aspect of Meto phonology. [Culhane & Edwards 2025: 169] || Stress in Meto is penultimate, but enclitics are extra-metrical and do not bear stress; e.g. Amfo'an ai ‘fire’ + =ees → /aidʒees/ [ˈʔaidʒɛs]. [Culhane & Edwards 2025: 173] || As in the Rote languages, content words are minimally disyllabic, stress is penultimate, and double vowels /ii/, /ee/, /aa/, /oo/ and /uu/ are realised phonetically as a single long vowel. [Edwards 2021: 36]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (1815 lines; PDF alongside). The passage is at lines 155-160, directly under the running head 'PARALLEL SOUND CORRESPONDENCES IN UAB METO 55', i.e. journal p. 55 / PDF page 4, section 2 'Uab Meto language background' as stated. Text reads: 'All known Uab Meto varieties have the ten consonants /p t k ʔ b f s h m n/4 and either of the liquids /r/ or /l/.5 In addition to these eleven consonants, the voiced obstruents /ʤ/ and /ɡ/ have a much more limited distribution.. (see 3.4.1).6 Known varieties of Uab Meto have the five vowels /i e a o u/.7 Word stress falls on the penultimate vowel. Vowel-initial words begin with a predictable glottal stop; /asu/ "dog" → [ˈʔasʊ]. While all Uab Meto…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the penultimate vowel (penultimate syllable) of the word in every known variety of the Meto/Uab Meto cluster, of which Baikeno is one; the same author's later works repeat this for Meto (Edwards 2021: 36 'stress is penultimate'; Culhane & Edwards 2025: 169 acoustic evidence for stress on the penultimate syllable, weight irrelevant; p.173 enclitics extra-metrical). Vowel sequences that count as one syllable (phonetic diphthongs/long vowels) take stress as a unit (Culhane 2024: 80; Edwards 2020: 111).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated in Edwards 2016 for Meto. For the closely related Amarasi variety Edwards 2020 (sec. 3.3.4, p.111) assigns secondary stress to every second syllable to the left of the primary; Culhane & Edwards 2025: 173 state enclitics are extra-metrical and unstressed in Meto.
new_statements.exceptions: None in Edwards 2016. Cluster-level sources note: words whose initial vowel sequence is a single phonetic syllable (e.g. aina-f 'mother', uaba-ʔ 'speech') are stressed on that syllable, analysed as still penultimate (Culhane 2024: 80; Edwards 2020: 111); Steinhauer 1996 (Nilulat dialect, uabm1237) notes a few stems with petrified prefixes stressed on the final syllable (PL A-84: 224).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('Word stress'); Culhane & Edwards 2025 make the prosodic word the domain with enclitics excluded; phrase-final stress is on the last prosodic word (Edwards 2020: 111-112, Amarasi).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statements are made for the whole Meto/Uab Meto cluster ('all known Uab Meto varieties', 'Known Meto varieties'), not for Baikeno alone. Baikeno (bkx, baik1238) is explicitly listed as one of the varieties whose data the authors use (Edwards 2016: 55; Edwards 2021 Table 2.2 p.34; Culhane & Edwards 2025: 168), and no Baikeno exception is noted, but no opened source describes Baikeno stress on its own. The acoustic evidence behind Culhane & Edwards 2025 comes from Amfo'an (amfo1237), and Steinhauer 1996 describes the Nilulat dialect (uabm1237), which is already in the catalog. Hull 2001 remains the only Baikeno-specific description and could not be opened.

new_statements.quote: p.398: "De stamwoorden zijn in het Timorees steeds tweesyllabig en de algemene regel is, dat de toon valt op de eerste syllabe, zoals reeds bleek uit de in het voorgaande gegeven voorbeelden. Op deze regel zijn enkele uitzonderingen. In de eerste plaats enkele ontleende woorden." p.399: "pèn-lèko bestaat uit pèna „mais" en lèko „goed"; ieder woord afzonderlijk heeft de nadruk op de eerste syllabe. [...] Indien echter een verbinding optreedt van een tweelettergrepig met een eenlettergrepig woord, heeft de eerste syllabe verzwakte en de laatste versterkte toon, bijv. anhesi (Amarasi) van anah = anhe, en si = één kind"
new_statements.translation: p.398: "Stem words in Timorese are always disyllabic and the general rule is that the stress falls on the first syllable, as was already apparent from the examples given above. There are a few exceptions to this rule. In the first place some borrowed words." p.399: "pèn-lèko consists of pèna 'maize' and lèko 'good'; each word on its own has the stress on the first syllable. [...] If, however, a disyllabic word is combined with a monosyllabic word, the first syllable has weakened and the last syllable strengthened stress, e.g. anhesi (Amarasi) from anah = anhe and si = one child."
new_statements.citation: Middelkoop, Pieter. 1950. Proeve van een Timorese grammatica. Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 106(3): 375-517.
new_statements.locator: p. 398-399, ch. II 'Het klanksysteem', section 7 'De klemtoon' (pp. 25-26); stress-shift example totiu p. 400

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's penultimate rule (Edwards 2016 'Word stress falls on the penultimate vowel' for all known Uab Meto varieties): for the always-disyllabic stems 'first syllable of the stem' = penultimate, and trisyllabic compounds are also penultimate. Adds detail the catalog lacks: compound stress (first member weakened), disyllable+monosyllable compounds with final prominence (anhesi etc.), and a list of lexical exceptions (loans with final stress, pa-/pe- words with 2nd-syllable stress, kolès/kalin/bukis). The framing is stem-initial rather than right-edge penultimate, but no placement conflict for native roots. Describes 'Timorees' of Dutch West Timor (Amarasi, Molo, Amanuba…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Middelkoop frames the rule from the stem: Timorese (Uab Meto) stems are always disyllabic and stress falls on the first syllable of the stem, i.e. the penultimate syllable of every root word. Trisyllabic words are compounds; the first member's stress is strongly weakened and full stress goes to the first syllable of the (disyllabic) second member (pèn-lèko -> stress on lè, nakfatu -> on fa), again penultimate. A disyllable + monosyllable compound has weakened stress on its first syllable and strengthened stress on its last (anhesi, elutu, lakatu, meopan, bauk'ulu, baspain), i.e. word-final prominence in those forms. He cites de Josselin de Jong (1937:178, on Kisar/Oirata) for the dislike of two fully stressed syllables in one word and says it holds for Timorese too.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not named as such; in compounds the first member keeps a 'strongly weakened' stress on its initial syllable while the last member carries full stress (pèn-lèko, nakfatu); hèlanlis has 'a light stress on the first and a strong stress on the last syllable'.
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords with final stress: kelak (< Du. klacht via Kupang Malay), filuil (< Mal. ferduli), hèlanlis (< Du. herendienst; light first, strong last); firu (< Mal. perlu) has regular initial stress; walnemen (< Du. waarnemend) stresses the 2nd syllable. A small set of pa-/pe- words with 2nd-syllable stress, apparently parsed as prefix pa- + stem: palak, palsai, palis, paleo, palkat; trisyllabic palkanis, paililu (< Port. perdido), polobliu (< Port. pulverino). Also sakan (final stress, sa- felt as prefix), kolès, kalin, bukis. Stress shift ('toonverspringing') in totiu 'rain bird' (< toti + oè) with full stress on ti. Possible stress-driven syncope mananu > mnanu, manane > mnane (p.400).
new_statements.identity_note: Middelkoop 1950 describes 'Timorees' (Uab Meto/Dawan) as spoken in Dutch West Timor, drawing chiefly on Amarasi and Molo with Amanuban, Amanatun, Amfo'an, Fatule'u and Kupang forms flagged; Baikeno/Ambenu/Oecusse (the Portuguese-Timor enclave variety, baik1238) is never named. Its stress statement is therefore language-cluster-level, on the same footing as the catalog record (Edwards 2016 'all known Uab Meto varieties', which does include Baikeno data), not a Baikeno-specific observation.

readall_conflicts: No placement conflict. Middelkoop 1950 (p.398) states stress on the first syllable of the always-disyllabic stem, which coincides with the catalog's penultimate rule (Edwards 2016, 2021; Culhane 2024; Culhane & Edwards 2025) for root words and for trisyllabic compounds (stress on the first syllable of the last disyllabic member = penult). Two wrinkles only Middelkoop records: (i) disyllable+monosyllable combinations carry strengthened stress on the LAST syllable (anhesi, elutu, lakatu, meopan, bauk'ulu, baspain), which a blanket penultimate rule would not predict; (ii) lexical exceptions -- loans with final stress (kelak, filuil, hèlanlis), pa-/pe- words with second-syllable stress (palak, palsai, palis, paleo, palkat), and kolès, kalin, bukis. These are refinements/exceptions, not a different stress type.
